title: SAT Reading & Writing
description: Free SAT Reading & Writing study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Information & Ideas

concepts.intro: Every SAT Reading passage (usually 25-150 words) has one controlling idea that everything else supports. The central-idea question asks what the passage as a whole is mainly about or trying to accomplish, not what any single sentence says.
b: Read the whole passage first; don't answer from the first sentence alone.
Ask 'what is this passage DOING' (arguing, explaining, describing, comparing) as well as what it's about.
The correct answer must be supported by the ENTIRE passage, not just part of it.
Eliminate answers that are too narrow (true of only one detail) or too broad (bring in outside claims).
Topic sentences and concluding sentences often signal the main idea, but short SAT passages can bury it mid-passage.
Restate the passage in your own one-sentence summary before looking at answer choices.

concepts.intro: Detail questions ask you to locate specific information the passage explicitly states, often phrased 'According to the text' or 'Based on the passage.'
b: These are the most literal questions on the test — the answer is stated, not implied.
Locate the exact line/phrase before choosing; do not rely on memory of the passage.
Watch for answer choices that use synonyms of the passage's wording (correct) vs. choices that reverse or distort a detail (wrong).
Beware 'half-right' answers that get one clause correct and the other clause wrong.
If two answers seem textually supported, pick the one that answers the exact question asked.

concepts.intro: Inference questions ask what the passage suggests or implies without stating directly. The correct inference is a small, logical step from the text — never a leap.
b: The right answer must be provable using only what's in the passage — no outside knowledge, no speculation.
Look for qualifying language in the passage (may, suggests, some researchers) — inferences often hinge on it.
Reject answer choices that are extreme ('always,' 'proves,' 'the only') when the passage is tentative.
A safe inference restates cause-and-effect or comparison relationships already implied by the passage's structure.
If an inference requires you to assume something not mentioned, it's wrong, however plausible it sounds.

concepts.intro: Purpose questions ask WHY the author included a sentence, detail, or the whole passage — to inform, persuade, illustrate, qualify, or contrast.
b: Identify the verb in the answer choice (illustrate, undermine, emphasize, concede) and check it matches the passage's function, not just its topic.
A quotation or example is usually included to support the point made in the surrounding sentences — trace it back to that claim.
Distinguish the author's own viewpoint from a viewpoint the author is describing or quoting (common trap in paired-perspective passages).
Tone words (skeptical, admiring, cautious, matter-of-fact) come from word choice, not the topic itself.

concepts.intro: Some questions ask which choice best restates a sentence or passage's content in different words — testing whether you tracked meaning, not just vocabulary.
b: A correct paraphrase preserves the logical relationship (cause, contrast, condition) of the original, not just its topic words.
Wrong paraphrases often flip a relationship — turning a cause into an effect, or a similarity into a contrast.
Strip out figurative or technical language mentally and restate the sentence in plain terms before comparing to choices.
Watch for choices that summarize accurately but add unsupported extra claims.

concepts.intro: Some Information & Ideas passages pair a short text with a table or graph; you must connect what the text claims to what the data actually shows.
b: Read the graph's axes, units, and labels before reading the surrounding text's claim about it.
Check whether the data supports, contradicts, or is irrelevant to the textual claim — all three appear as trap patterns.
Note the exact data range or group described in the text; graphs often contain more categories/years than the claim covers.
Answers that require interpolating beyond the graph's shown range are unsupported — reject them.

keyFacts: Read the full short passage before touching the answer choices — SAT Reading passages are dense, and the first sentence rarely contains the whole main idea.
Predict an answer in your own words before reading the choices; this prevents being talked into a trap answer.
Every correct answer on Information & Ideas questions must be directly supported by the passage text — never by outside knowledge.
Process of elimination beats searching for the 'perfect' answer — cross out anything unsupported, extreme, or off-topic first.
traps: Choosing an answer that is true in the real world but not stated in the passage, not stated in the passage.
Picking an answer that restates one detail instead of the passage's overall main idea, overall main idea.
Selecting an extreme-language choice ('proves,' 'always,' 'completely') when the passage only hints or qualifies, only hints or qualifies.
Confusing the author's own opinion with a view the author is merely summarizing or quoting, merely summarizing or quoting.

units.name: Command of Evidence

concepts.intro: These paired-format questions ask which quotation or line from the passage best supports the answer to a previous question, or best supports a given claim.
b: Answer the claim/question first in your own words, THEN find the line that proves it — don't hunt for evidence before you know what you're proving.
The best evidence directly states the claim; it doesn't just relate to the same topic.
Eliminate quotations that support a DIFFERENT, related claim — a classic wrong-answer pattern.
If a quotation only partially supports the claim, keep checking — a fuller match is usually available.
On the digital SAT, evidence questions are single questions (not two-part) — the quotation is baked into the answer choices as bracketed text.

concepts.intro: Command of Evidence also includes questions where you must pick the data point, from a table or graph, that best supports or completes an argument in the passage.
b: Identify exactly what variable and unit the claim is about before scanning the data.
Check every row/column carefully — answers often swap two categories or two years that look similar.
A correct data answer must be consistent with the direction of the claim (increase vs. decrease, higher vs. lower).
Reject data points that are true but don't address the specific comparison the claim makes.
For 'which finding would most strengthen/weaken' questions, decide strengthen or weaken conceptually first, then look for matching data.

concepts.intro: Some questions give a hypothesis or claim and ask which fact, if true, would most support it or most weaken it.
b: A weakening fact usually introduces an alternative explanation, an exception, or a missing condition.
A supporting fact usually shows the predicted result actually occurred, or rules out an alternative cause.
Irrelevant-but-true facts are the most common wrong answer — they don't logically bear on the claim at all.
Watch for facts that support the OPPOSITE of what's asked (a classic reversed-logic trap).

concepts.l: Selecting the Best Evidence Among Similar Options
concepts.intro: When two or more answer choices seem to relate to the correct claim, the SAT rewards precision — the tightest logical fit wins.
b: Compare each candidate quotation against the EXACT wording of the claim, not just its general subject.
A quotation that provides an example is stronger evidence than one that merely mentions the topic in passing.
General background information is rarely 'the best evidence' — specific findings or direct statements usually are.
Double-check quantifiers ('some,' 'most,' 'all') in the quotation match the quantifiers in the claim.

concepts.intro: The digital SAT tests whether you can reason carefully about data, not just read a chart.
b: Correlation shown in data does not by itself prove causation — reject answers that claim one variable 'causes' another unless the passage states it.
A single data point is not a trend — don't accept an answer that generalizes from one year/sample to 'always' or 'increasingly.'
Sample size and scope matter: a claim about 'all teenagers' isn't supported by data from one school.
Percentage change and absolute change are different — misreading one for the other is a frequent trap.

keyFacts: Always answer the underlying question first, then match it to evidence — never evidence-shop before you know your claim.
The correct evidence choice proves the SPECIFIC claim asked about, not just a related idea from the same passage.
For data questions, identify the exact variables and direction (more/less, before/after) the claim needs before scanning the graph.
When strengthening/weakening a claim, decide the logical relationship first, then find the fact that matches it.
traps: Picking a quotation that's on-topic but proves a different point than the one asked about, than the one asked about.
Treating correlation in a graph as proof of causation, as proof of causation.
Choosing evidence that is true but too general to actually support the specific claim, to actually support the specific claim.
Misreading which direction (increase vs. decrease) the data or claim is going, the data or claim is going.

units.name: Words in Context

concepts.intro: Words-in-Context questions ask you to choose the word/phrase that best completes a sentence with a blank, or to determine the meaning of a word as used in the passage.
b: Cover the answer choices, read the sentence, and predict your own word for the blank before looking at options.
Match your prediction's MEANING to a choice — the correct answer is often a less common synonym, not the obvious word.
Context clues live in the same sentence or nearby sentences: look for contrast words (but, although, yet) and continuation words (moreover, similarly).
The right answer must fit both the meaning AND the grammar/register of the sentence (formal essay vs. casual quote).
Don't pick a word just because it's a word you know well — SAT often uses uncommon synonyms of common ideas.

concepts.intro: Many wrong choices are near-synonyms with the wrong connotation (positive/negative/neutral) or wrong intensity for the context.
b: Determine whether the sentence's tone is positive, negative, or neutral before matching connotation.
'Reluctant' and 'refusing' both mean unwilling, but differ in degree — match the intensity the context implies.
Watch for words that sound sophisticated but subtly shift meaning (e.g., 'notorious' vs. 'famous').
Eliminate any choice that would be a true statement but wrong tone (too harsh or too mild) for the passage's context.

concepts.intro: Logical transition words inside or around the blank sentence often ARE the context clue that determines the correct word.
b: 'However/but/yet' signals the blank should contrast with a nearby idea.
'Moreover/similarly/likewise' signals the blank should continue or reinforce a nearby idea.
'Because/since/therefore' signals a cause-effect relationship the word must fit.
If the sentence structure is 'not X but rather Y,' the blank's meaning is opposite of X.

concepts.intro: Some tested words are common but have a less-common secondary meaning that fits the specific passage context.
b: Words like 'novel' (new vs. a book), 'sound' (healthy/valid vs. noise), 'grave' (serious vs. burial site) can trip you up if you jump to the first meaning you think of.
Always re-derive the meaning from the sentence's own context — never from the word's most common definition.
If your first-instinct answer isn't offered, reread the sentence for a less common sense of the word.

concepts.intro: Words-in-Context also tests whether a word fits the formality and attitude of the passage as a whole (academic, journalistic, personal narrative).
b: Academic/scientific passages favor precise, neutral, technical word choices.
A quoted speaker's own words may be more casual than the surrounding academic narration — match register to the exact spot in the sentence.
Overly emotional or colloquial choices are usually wrong in formal expository passages.

keyFacts: Always predict your own word before reading the answer choices — this prevents being misled by attractive-sounding wrong options.
Context clues (contrast/continuation/cause-effect transitions) in the same or nearby sentence determine the correct meaning.
Match connotation and intensity, not just literal meaning — many wrong choices are 'close but too strong/weak.'
For multiple-meaning words, always derive meaning from the sentence's specific context, never from the word's most common definition.
traps: Picking the most familiar meaning of a word instead of the meaning that fits this specific context, that fits this specific context.
Choosing a synonym with the wrong connotation or intensity for the sentence's tone, for the sentence's tone.
Ignoring a contrast or continuation transition word that determines the blank's required meaning, that determines the blank's required meaning.
Selecting a word that matches the topic but not the grammatical fit of the sentence, but not the grammatical fit of the sentence.

units.name: Expression of Ideas

concepts.intro: You're given bulleted notes on a topic and a stated goal (e.g., 'to compare two findings'), then asked which sentence best accomplishes that goal using only the given information.
b: Identify the exact goal verb: compare, contrast, introduce, explain a reason, emphasize a similarity/difference.
Use ONLY the facts given in the bullets — never add outside knowledge, even if true.
Eliminate choices that state facts accurately but don't accomplish the specific stated goal.
Eliminate choices that use only one bullet when the goal requires combining two.
A correct synthesis sentence is grammatically smooth and logically connects the chosen facts with an appropriate transition.

concepts.intro: Transition questions ask you to pick the word/phrase that correctly signals the logical relationship between two sentences or clauses.
b: First determine the actual relationship: contrast, cause-effect, addition, example, sequence, or concession.
Contrast: however, nevertheless, on the other hand, in contrast, yet.
Cause-effect: therefore, thus, consequently, as a result.
Addition/continuation: moreover, furthermore, in addition, similarly.
Example: for instance, for example, specifically.
Read both surrounding sentences fully before choosing — the relationship is often not what the first sentence alone suggests.

concepts.intro: The SAT rewards clear, economical writing — when all else is equal, the most concise grammatically correct option is best.
b: Cut answer choices that repeat an idea already stated elsewhere in the sentence (e.g., 'return back,' 'each individual person').
Concise is only correct if it's also grammatically complete and doesn't lose necessary meaning.
Wordy phrases like 'due to the fact that' can usually be replaced by 'because' with no meaning loss.
Don't confuse 'shorter' with 'correct' — a short choice with a grammar error is still wrong.

concepts.l: Adding, Revising, or Deleting a Sentence
concepts.intro: These questions ask whether a proposed sentence should be added (or is effectively added) based on whether it fulfills a stated purpose.
b: Always check the STATED purpose in the question stem — 'yes' answers must actually achieve that purpose, not just be true information.
A sentence can be accurate and on-topic yet still 'No' because it doesn't fulfill the specific purpose asked about.
Consider whether the addition disrupts the paragraph's flow or duplicates a point already made.
For deletion questions, check whether removing the sentence loses a detail that a later sentence depends on.

concepts.intro: Some questions ask you to combine two short sentences effectively, testing subordination, coordination, and modifier placement.
b: Subordinating conjunctions (although, because, while, since) show one idea depends on/relates to another.
Coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join two independent, equally weighted clauses.
Combine using a participial phrase (e.g., 'Having finished the report, she left') only when the modifier clearly refers to the subject that follows.
Avoid choices that create a misplaced modifier, a comma splice, or a sentence fragment when combining.

keyFacts: For rhetorical synthesis, reread the stated goal verb before picking — many wrong answers are true but off-goal.
Determine the logical relationship (contrast, cause, addition) between ideas before selecting a transition word.
Prefer the most concise, grammatically correct option, but never sacrifice correctness for brevity.
For add/delete/revise questions, judge choices against the stated purpose, not just factual accuracy.
traps: Choosing a transition that fits the topic but signals the wrong logical relationship, the wrong logical relationship.
Picking a rhetorical synthesis sentence that's accurate but doesn't fulfill the specific stated goal, the specific stated goal.
Selecting the shortest option even though it contains a grammar error, contains a grammar error.
Adding outside knowledge not present in the given bullet points during synthesis questions, in the given bullet points during synthesis questions.

units.name: Standard English Conventions

concepts.intro: The verb must agree in number with its TRUE subject, even when other words or phrases sit between them.
b: Find the true subject by mentally deleting prepositional phrases and interrupters: 'The list of items (is/are) long' → subject is 'list' → 'is.'
Collective nouns (team, committee, group) are usually singular in American English: 'The team is winning.'
Compound subjects joined by 'and' are plural; joined by 'or/nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
Indefinite pronouns like 'each,' 'everyone,' 'neither' are singular: 'Each of the students has a book.'
A subject following 'there is/there are' still determines the verb: 'There are three reasons.'

concepts.intro: Punctuation questions test whether you know exactly what structure each mark requires.
b: Comma: separates items in a list, joins two independent clauses only WITH a FANBOYS conjunction, sets off nonessential (nonrestrictive) clauses/phrases.
Semicolon: joins two independent clauses with no conjunction, or separates items in a complex list that already contains commas.
Colon: follows a complete independent clause and introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration — never follows an incomplete phrase.
Essential (restrictive) clauses ('that,' defining who/which one) take NO commas; nonessential ('which,' extra info) DO take commas.
Dashes can substitute for commas or colons to set off nonessential info or introduce elaboration, often more emphatically.

concepts.intro: One of the most heavily tested conventions rules: recognizing when two clauses are improperly joined or a group of words isn't a complete sentence.
b: A comma splice = two independent clauses joined by only a comma: 'It rained, we stayed inside.' — WRONG.
Fix a splice with: a period, a semicolon, a comma + FANBOYS conjunction, or a subordinating conjunction.
A run-on has two independent clauses with NO punctuation at all between them — same fixes apply.
A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or is a subordinate clause standing alone: 'Because it rained.' is a fragment.
Test independence: can the clause stand alone as a full sentence? If yes, it's independent; if no, it's dependent/subordinate.

concepts.intro: Items in a list, comparison, or joined by a conjunction must share the same grammatical form.
b: In a list: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike' is WRONG — should be 'hiking, swimming, and biking.'
With correlative conjunctions (either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also), the grammatical structure after each half must match.
In comparisons ('more X than Y'), X and Y must be the same type of grammatical element.
Parallel structure also applies to verb tense consistency across a list of actions.

concepts.intro: Pronouns must agree in number and gender with their antecedent, and must use the correct case (subject/object/possessive).
b: A pronoun's antecedent must be clear and unambiguous — if a sentence could refer to two different nouns, it's an error.

Singular antecedents (everyone, each, a person) take singular pronouns; in modern usage 'they' is accepted as a singular gender-neutral pronoun on some style guides, but SAT favors clear singular/plural matching.
Subject pronouns (I, he, she, they, who) function as the sentence's subject; object pronouns (me, him, her, them, whom) function as objects.
'Who' refers to the subject of a clause; 'whom' refers to the object; test by substituting he/him.
Possessive pronouns (its, their, whose) never take an apostrophe; 'it's' = 'it is,' 'who's' = 'who is.'

concepts.intro: Verbs across a sentence or passage should stay in a logically consistent tense unless the meaning requires a shift.
b: Don't shift from past to present tense mid-sentence without a reason tied to the timeline of events.
The passage's established time frame (signaled by dates or context) tells you which tense is correct throughout.
The subjunctive mood is used for hypotheticals/wishes contrary to fact: 'If I were you' (not 'was').
Perfect tenses (has/have/had + past participle) show an action completed relative to another point in time — used to show sequence of past events.

keyFacts: Always find the TRUE subject of a verb by ignoring interrupting prepositional phrases before checking agreement.
A comma alone can never join two independent clauses — that's a comma splice, one of the most common SAT errors.
Essential (that/no commas) vs. nonessential (which/commas) clauses is a frequently tested distinction.
Items joined in a list or by correlative conjunctions must share identical grammatical form (parallel structure).
traps: Matching a verb to a noun in an interrupting phrase instead of to the true subject, instead of to the true subject.
Joining two independent clauses with just a comma (comma splice) instead of a semicolon or comma+conjunction, instead of a semicolon or comma+conjunction.
Adding a comma before an essential 'that' clause that should have no comma at all, that should have no comma at all.
Breaking parallel structure by mixing verb forms (gerund vs. infinitive) in a list, in a list.

units.name: Science Passages

concepts.intro: Science passages typically follow a predictable structure: background/problem, hypothesis or research question, method, findings, and interpretation/implications.
b: Identify which structural stage each sentence belongs to as you read — this helps you locate answers fast.
The hypothesis is a prediction; the findings are what actually happened; don't confuse the two in answer choices.
Interpretation/implication sentences often use hedged language ('suggests,' 'may indicate') — treat these as less certain than stated findings.
A passage may describe a surprising or unexpected result — the 'why it matters' sentence usually follows immediately after.

concepts.intro: Some questions test whether you understand what a study's design can and cannot prove, including variables and controls.
b: Identify the independent variable (what's manipulated) and dependent variable (what's measured) in the described experiment.
A control group isolates the effect of the independent variable by holding other conditions constant.
A correlational (observational) study cannot establish causation the way a controlled experiment can — watch for this distinction in answer choices.
Confounding variables are alternate explanations a weak experimental design fails to rule out.

concepts.l: Interpreting Data (Graphs, Tables) in Science Passages
concepts.intro: Science passages are the most likely to pair text with quantitative data — reading the graph correctly is as important as reading the prose.
b: Check axis labels and units first; a common trap answer misreads the unit (e.g., confusing percentage with raw count).
Identify the trend (increasing, decreasing, plateauing, cyclical) before matching to a textual claim about it.
Outliers or exceptions in the data are frequently the basis of an 'except' or 'best supports' question.
When a question asks which data point would strengthen/weaken a hypothesis, check if the point is consistent with the DIRECTION the hypothesis predicts.

concepts.intro: Science passages often define an unfamiliar or technical term within the passage itself — you're tested on using that in-context definition, not outside knowledge.
b: The passage usually defines or illustrates a technical term nearby (an appositive, a following sentence, or an example) — use that instead of prior knowledge.
Don't let real-world science knowledge override what the specific passage states; the SAT tests reading comprehension, not science facts.
Words like 'significant' have a technical statistical meaning (unlikely due to chance) that differs from everyday 'important' — watch for this in science contexts.

concepts.intro: Science writing frequently explains WHY something happens (mechanism) as distinct from simply stating THAT it happens (observation).
b: Distinguish a stated observation ('X increased') from a proposed explanation for it ('researchers believe this occurred because...').
Multiple competing explanations may be presented — track which one the author actually endorses versus merely reports.
Look for signal phrases: 'due to,' 'as a result of,' 'this is thought to occur because' introduce mechanism explanations.

keyFacts: Science passages follow background → hypothesis → method → findings → interpretation; locate answers by structural stage.
Never substitute outside science knowledge for the passage's own in-context definitions or findings.
Correlational data alone cannot prove causation — a frequent basis for 'weakens the claim' answers.
Always check graph axis units and labels before matching data to a textual claim.
traps: Confusing what a hypothesis predicted with what the results actually showed, what the results actually showed.
Assuming a correlational study proves causation when the passage doesn't claim that, when the passage doesn't claim that.
Relying on outside science knowledge instead of the passage's own stated definition of a term, instead of the passage's own stated definition of a term.
Misreading a graph's units (percentage vs. raw count, or per-year vs. cumulative), percentage vs. raw count, or per-year vs. cumulative.

units.name: History/Social Studies Passages

concepts.intro: History/Social Studies passages include excerpts from historical documents (primary sources) and modern scholarly commentary (secondary sources) — often with older or more formal diction.
b: Don't let unfamiliar older vocabulary or syntax stop you — restate dense sentences in plain modern language as you read.
Identify who is speaking (the historical author) and what their stated position or purpose is.
A secondary-source passage analyzing a primary source will state its own claim about that source — separate the source's content from the analyst's interpretation.
Historical context clues (dates, named events, institutions) help you infer the stakes of an argument even without outside knowledge.

concepts.intro: Many history/social studies passages are persuasive essays or speeches — understanding their argumentative moves is key.
b: Identify the claim, the reasons given, and any counterargument the author addresses or concedes.
A concession ('while it is true that...') followed by 'but/however' shows the author acknowledges an opposing point before refuting it.
Rhetorical questions, repetition, and appeals to shared values are persuasive techniques the SAT may ask you to identify by function.
Distinguish evidence (facts, examples, data) from the claim it supports — evidence questions often follow argument passages.

concepts.intro: Understanding the social or political moment referenced helps determine an author's stance and purpose, even from a short excerpt.
b: Look for framing words revealing stance: reformer, critic, advocate, skeptic — often stated directly in an introductory note.
The SAT provides any necessary historical background in the passage itself or a brief intro line — you never need outside historical knowledge to answer.
An author writing 'in response to' or 'in defense of' something signals the passage is reactive/persuasive rather than purely descriptive.

concepts.intro: Some questions present two short passages or two viewpoints on the same historical/social topic and ask how they relate.
b: Identify each passage's central claim independently before comparing them.
Determine whether the passages agree, directly disagree, or address different aspects of the same issue (a common 'nuance' trap).
Passage-comparison questions often ask how the author of Passage 2 would likely respond to a claim in Passage 1 — base this ONLY on stated views, not assumption.
Watch for a shared premise the passages agree on even while disagreeing on the conclusion.

concepts.l: Tone, Bias, and Persuasive Word Choice
concepts.intro: History/Social Studies passages are evaluated for how word choice reveals the author's attitude toward the subject.
b: Loaded words (regime vs. government, scheme vs. plan) reveal bias — identify their connotation.
An objective/neutral tone uses precise, unemotional language even when describing controversial topics.
A passage can present a claim it ultimately criticizes — track whose viewpoint a sentence expresses before judging author tone.

keyFacts: You never need outside historical knowledge — all context necessary to answer is in the passage or its intro line.
Separate what a quoted historical figure says from what the passage's own analysis says about them.
In paired passages, determine each passage's claim independently before comparing agreement/disagreement.
Identify claim → reason → counterargument/concession structure in persuasive history passages.
traps: Assuming outside historical knowledge is needed when the passage/intro already supplies the needed context, already supplies the needed context.
Mixing up the historical speaker's viewpoint with the modern author's analytical viewpoint, with the modern author's analytical viewpoint.
Treating two paired passages as fully agreeing when they only share one narrow premise, when they only share one narrow premise.
Missing a concession ('while... however') and thinking the author holds the conceded view, thinking the author holds the conceded view.

units.name: Pacing & Strategy

concepts.intro: The digital SAT Reading & Writing section has two modules of 27 questions each in 32 minutes (about 71 seconds/question), and module 2's difficulty adapts based on module 1 performance.
b: Aim for roughly 60-75 seconds per question on average; some questions (grammar) go faster, leaving buffer for longer reading questions.
Module 1 performance determines whether Module 2 is the harder or easier variant — there's no way to 'skip ahead,' so treat every Module 1 question with full effort.
Because it's adaptive, you cannot go back to a previous MODULE once submitted, but you CAN move between questions within the current module.
Track time at the quarter-marks (roughly question 7, 14, 20) to catch yourself falling behind early rather than at the end.

concepts.intro: Not all questions deserve equal time investment — recognizing when to flag and move on protects your overall score.
b: If a question is taking more than ~90 seconds with no progress, flag it and move on; return at the end if time allows.
Grammar/convention questions are often the fastest points on the test — do not lose time on them by overanalyzing.
Long or dense passages with a straightforward detail question can be answered by scanning for a keyword instead of rereading everything.
Never leave a question blank on the digital SAT — there's no penalty for guessing, so always select an answer before time runs out.

concepts.l: Process of Elimination Under Time Pressure
concepts.intro: Eliminating clearly wrong answers quickly is often faster than trying to 'prove' the right answer directly, especially under time pressure.
b: Cross off any answer that contradicts explicit text, uses extreme language unsupported by the passage, or is off-topic.
For grammar questions, first check if there's an obvious agreement/punctuation error in three of the four choices.
When down to two choices, reread the specific line(s) in question rather than the whole passage again.
Trust textual evidence over 'this sounds right' instinct — SAT wrong answers are designed to sound plausible.

concepts.intro: With dozens of short, dense passages back-to-back, maintaining focus across the whole module affects accuracy more than raw reading speed.
b: Take a 2-3 second mental reset between questions — treat each passage as a fresh start, not a continuation of the last one's topic.
If you catch yourself re-reading the same sentence three times, it usually means you skimmed too fast the first time — slow down deliberately.
Save your slowest, most careful reading for rhetorical synthesis and inference questions — they reward precision most.
Physical resets (sit up, breathe, unclench) between passages help sustain concentration through a ~32-minute module.

concepts.intro: Digital SAT allows reviewing and changing answers within the current module before time expires or you submit.
b: Use the on-screen review page to confirm every question has an answer selected before submitting the module.
Revisit flagged questions first with remaining time, using fresh eyes rather than immediately re-reading your first attempt's reasoning.
Don't second-guess grammar answers you were confident about on first pass — changing answers without new evidence often hurts more than helps.
If time is nearly out, guess strategically on remaining flagged items rather than leaving any blank.

keyFacts: Digital SAT R&W has 2 modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each — average pace is about 60-75 seconds per question.
Module 2's difficulty is determined by Module 1 performance; you cannot revisit a module once it's submitted.
There is no guessing penalty — never leave any question blank.
Flag genuinely hard questions and return to them at the end rather than burning time on a single item early.
traps: Spending too long perfecting an early hard question and running out of time for easier later ones, and running out of time for easier later ones.
Leaving a question blank instead of guessing when time runs low, instead of guessing when time runs low.
Changing a confident grammar answer during review without any new textual reason, without any new textual reason.
Rereading an entire passage from scratch instead of scanning for the specific line a question references, instead of scanning for the specific line a question references.

quiz.q: The city library extended its weekend hours after a survey showed most visitors worked full-time jobs during weekday hours. Which choice best states the main idea?
o: The library survey was poorly designed.
The library changed its hours in response to visitor feedback about scheduling conflicts.
The library plans to close on weekends.
quiz.e: The text says hours were extended because most visitors couldn't come during weekday hours -- a direct response to a scheduling conflict.

quiz.q: A restaurant switched to a reservation-only model after years of long walk-in wait times. Since the change, customer complaints about wait times have dropped by half, though a few regulars have complained about the new booking requirement. Which is the most reasonable inference?
o: The reservation system eliminated all customer complaints.
The reservation system solved the wait-time problem for most customers but introduced a different frustration for some.
The restaurant lost most of its regular customers.
Walk-in customers are no longer allowed at the restaurant.
quiz.e: Complaints about wait time dropped (solved for most) while a new complaint (booking) appeared for a subset (regulars) -- a trade-off, not total elimination or an outright ban implied.

quiz.q: Researchers studying a remote lake found that its water clarity had improved over ten years, coinciding with a local ban on phosphate-based fertilizers upstream. They caution, however, that other factors, such as reduced rainfall, may also have contributed. Which choice best describes the researchers' claim?
o: The fertilizer ban is definitely the sole cause of improved clarity.
The fertilizer ban may be one of several contributing factors to improved clarity.
Reduced rainfall is the only explanation for improved clarity.
Water clarity has not actually improved.
quiz.e: The passage explicitly hedges ("may also have contributed"), so the researchers claim a possible, not sole, cause.

quiz.q: A museum director noted that attendance rose sharply after a new admission-by-donation policy was introduced, but revenue per visitor fell. The director stated the museum would continue the policy "because our mission is public access, not profit." Based on the text, which is most strongly supported?
o: The museum plans to end the donation policy soon.
The director values increased public access over maximizing revenue.
Attendance actually declined under the new policy.
quiz.e: The director's stated reasoning ("mission is public access, not profit") directly supports valuing access over revenue, despite falling per-visitor revenue.

quiz.q: A claim states that a new traffic light pattern reduced accidents at a busy intersection. Which finding would most directly support this claim?
o: The intersection is used by more cars than any other in the city.
The number of accidents at the intersection dropped by 40% in the year after the new pattern was installed.
The city spent $50,000 installing the new traffic lights.
Drivers reported the new lights were easier to see at night.
quiz.e: A direct before/after drop in accidents is the most direct evidence for the claim; cost, traffic volume, and visibility comments don't measure accident rates.

quiz.q: A dietitian claims that skipping breakfast leads to overeating later in the day. Which finding would most seriously undermine this claim?
o: Participants who skipped breakfast consumed roughly the same total daily calories as those who ate breakfast.
Some participants skipped breakfast only on weekends.
Breakfast foods vary widely in nutritional content.
The study included both adults and teenagers.
quiz.e: If total daily calories were roughly the same regardless of breakfast, that directly contradicts the claim that skipping breakfast causes overeating later.

quiz.q: A claim states that a company's new recycling program reduced landfill waste. Which finding would most directly support this claim?
o: The company hired five new employees for the program.
The amount of waste sent to the landfill decreased by 30% after the program began.
The program was announced in a company newsletter.
Employees were given reusable water bottles.
quiz.e: A direct decrease in landfill waste after the program began is the most relevant, direct evidence for a claim about reduced waste.

quiz.q: A teacher claims that using flashcards improves vocabulary retention more than reading a word list. Which study result would best support this claim?
o: Students who used flashcards scored higher on a retention test one week later than students who only read the word list.
Both groups of students found the material moderately difficult.
Students who used flashcards reported enjoying the activity.
quiz.e: A direct, measured difference in retention test scores between the two methods is the clearest support for the comparative claim.

quiz.q: An economist argues that a minimum wage increase in a city led to job losses in the restaurant industry. Which finding would most directly challenge this argument?
o: Restaurant employment in the city grew at the same rate as in nearby cities without a wage increase.
The city's population grew during the same period.
Some restaurants raised their menu prices.
The minimum wage increase was announced a year in advance.
quiz.e: If employment grew at the SAME rate as cities without any wage increase, that suggests the wage increase itself wasn't the cause of any job change -- directly challenging the causal claim.

quiz.q: A claim states that a species of bird has adapted its migration timing in response to warming temperatures. Which evidence would most directly support this claim?
o: The bird species is found on multiple continents.
Long-term records show the birds now migrate an average of two weeks earlier than they did 40 years ago, coinciding with rising regional temperatures.
The bird's diet consists mainly of insects.
Bird watchers have reported sightings in new areas.
quiz.e: A documented shift in migration timing that coincides with the proposed cause (warming) is direct, relevant support; the other options don't address timing or its cause.

quiz.q: The volunteers' efforts were largely ______, receiving little public recognition despite the significant impact of their work. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: "Little public recognition" directly matches "unheralded" (not celebrated or announced); the other options don't fit that description.

quiz.q: Unlike her usually ______ writing style, the author's latest novel was sparse and direct, surprising longtime readers. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: The novel is described as "sparse and direct," in contrast to her USUAL style -- so the usual style must be the opposite: elaborate/"ornate."

quiz.q: The scientist remained ______ about the results, noting that a single study rarely proves a hypothesis conclusively. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: Noting that one study "rarely proves" something conclusively signals a careful, measured attitude -- "cautious" fits; the others don't match that reasoning.

quiz.q: The committee's decision was widely seen as ______, reversing a policy it had strongly defended just months earlier. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: Reversing a strongly-defended policy "just months" later is a sudden change -- "abrupt" fits; the others suggest continuity or expectedness, the opposite.

quiz.q: Rather than confronting the criticism directly, the executive offered a ______ response that neither confirmed nor denied the allegations. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: "Neither confirmed nor denied" describes a deliberately vague, non-committal response -- "evasive" fits precisely.

quiz.q: The professor's lecture was praised for its ______ approach, weaving together ideas from physics, philosophy, and art history into a single coherent argument. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: Weaving together multiple different fields (physics, philosophy, art history) into one argument describes an "interdisciplinary" approach.

quiz.q: The startup's first product failed to gain traction with consumers. ______, the company pivoted to a business-to-business model, which proved far more successful. Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
quiz.e: A failure followed by a company's reaction to it (pivoting) fits "In response"; the other options don't capture a cause-then-reaction relationship.

quiz.q: The proposed highway expansion promised to reduce commute times for suburban drivers. ______, environmental groups warned it would increase traffic and pollution in nearby neighborhoods. Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
quiz.e: Two opposing perspectives (promised benefit vs. warned-of harm) call for a contrast transition: "However."

quiz.q:
A student has gathered the following notes about two invasive plant species:
- Species A spreads primarily through windborne seeds and can colonize new areas quickly.
- Species A is toxic to most local wildlife that might otherwise eat it.
- Species B spreads through root fragments and grows slowly.
- Species B provides some nutritional value to a few local insect species.
The student wants to explain why Species A poses a more urgent ecological threat. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Species A spreads quickly via windborne seeds and is toxic to local wildlife, while Species B spreads slowly and provides some nutritional value to local insects.
Species B spreads through root fragments, unlike Species A.
Both Species A and Species B are considered invasive.
Species A's seeds are carried by wind.
quiz.e: Only this choice combines BOTH relevant facts about Species A (fast spread + toxicity) to explain urgency, contrasted with Species B's slower, less harmful profile -- directly answering "why more urgent."

quiz.q:
A student has gathered the following notes about a city's public transit ridership:
- Bus ridership increased 12% after fare-free days were introduced on weekends.
- Weekday ridership stayed flat during the same period.
- A rider survey found 68% of new weekend riders said cost was their main reason for not riding before.
- The transit agency has not yet studied the program's effect on overall city traffic.
The student wants to argue that the fare-free weekend program specifically addressed a cost barrier for potential riders. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: The transit agency has not studied the program's effect on traffic.
Weekend ridership rose 12%, and most new riders cited cost as the reason they hadn't ridden before -- directly linking the fare change to increased ridership.
Weekday ridership stayed the same during the study period.
Bus fares vary depending on the time of day.
quiz.e: Only this choice connects the ridership increase specifically to riders' own stated reason (cost) -- directly supporting the argument that the program addressed a cost barrier.

quiz.q: Critics initially dismissed the architect's design as impractical, citing its unconventional angles and reliance on unproven materials. ______, the building has since won multiple awards for both its structural innovation and energy efficiency. Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
quiz.e: Initial dismissal followed by later acclaim is a contrast -- "Yet" fits; "Consequently" would wrongly suggest the awards resulted from the criticism.

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

The conference featured speakers from four countries______ Japan, Brazil, Kenya, and Canada.
quiz.e: A colon correctly introduces a list elaborating on "four countries"; a semicolon would require an independent clause after it.

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

The experiment's results, while promising______ require further testing before any conclusions can be drawn.
quiz.e: "While promising" is a modifying phrase interrupting the main clause ("The experiment's results... require further testing"); a single comma correctly sets it off before the verb resumes.

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

The team of researchers, along with their lab assistants, ______ preparing the final report.
quiz.e: The subject is "team" (singular); "along with their lab assistants" is a modifying phrase, not part of the compound subject. The verb agrees with "team": "is."

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

One of the primary reasons for the delay ______ the unexpected shortage of building materials.
quiz.e: The subject is "One" (singular), not "reasons"; the verb should be "was."

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

The applicant's resume listed several qualifications______ a degree in engineering, five years of industry experience, and fluency in three languages.
quiz.e: "Including" correctly introduces examples within the same sentence, and the comma before it matches standard usage for this construction.

quiz.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

Either the manager or her assistants ______ responsible for approving the request.
quiz.e: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the noun closer to it -- "assistants" (plural) -- so "are" is correct.

quiz.q: A study of hibernating ground squirrels found that their body temperature drops to nearly match the surrounding environment during winter dormancy, yet their brain activity briefly spikes every few weeks in short arousal periods. Which choice best states the main point of the text?
o: Ground squirrels do not survive most winters.
Hibernation in ground squirrels involves nearly matching environmental temperature, punctuated by periodic brief arousals.
Ground squirrels are more active in winter than in summer.
Brain activity in ground squirrels is constant throughout hibernation.
quiz.e: The text describes two specific features of hibernation: temperature matching AND periodic arousal spikes -- the main point covers both, not survival rates or constant activity.

quiz.q: Because the newly discovered bacterium can survive extreme heat, cold, and radiation, researchers described it as remarkably ______. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: Surviving extreme heat, cold, AND radiation describes toughness -- "resilient" fits; "fragile" is the opposite.

quiz.q: A marine biologist notes that coral reefs near a certain island have shown no signs of bleaching despite regional ocean temperatures rising by 1.5C over the past decade -- a temperature increase that has caused significant bleaching elsewhere. The biologist is now studying whether this reef's coral has a unique genetic trait. Based on the text, which is the most reasonable inference?
o: All coral reefs worldwide are resistant to bleaching.
The reef's resistance to bleaching under conditions that harm coral elsewhere suggests some distinguishing factor may be involved.
Ocean temperatures near the island have not actually risen.
Coral bleaching is not related to temperature.
quiz.e: The reef surviving conditions that cause bleaching ELSEWHERE, combined with the biologist actively investigating a genetic explanation, supports that SOME distinguishing factor is likely -- not a universal claim about all reefs.

quiz.q: A researcher claims that a particular fungus helps plant roots absorb more phosphorus from soil. Which finding would most directly support this claim?
o: The fungus is found in soils around the world.
Plants grown with the fungus present absorbed 40% more phosphorus than plants grown without it, under otherwise identical conditions.
The fungus is difficult to cultivate in a laboratory.
Phosphorus is an essential nutrient for plant growth.
quiz.e: A controlled comparison showing a direct measured increase in phosphorus absorption, with other conditions held constant, is the clearest supporting evidence.

quiz.q: In the years following the introduction of a national postal service, letter-writing between distant relatives increased dramatically, and historians have since used surviving letters as a major source for understanding daily life of the period. Which choice best states the main idea?
o: The postal service was expensive to maintain.
The new postal service enabled a rise in letter-writing that later became a valuable historical resource.
Historians prefer letters to other historical sources.
Distant relatives rarely communicated before the postal service existed.
quiz.e: The text links the postal service to increased letter-writing, and notes those letters later served historians -- the main idea connects both facts.

quiz.q: A historian notes that a 19th-century trade agreement between two nations was renewed three times despite repeated public criticism in both countries. Based on the text, which is the most reasonable inference?
o: Despite public criticism, each government found enough benefit in the agreement to continue renewing it.
The agreement was renewed against both governments' wishes.
Public opinion had no role in trade policy at the time.
quiz.e: Repeated renewal despite criticism suggests the governments found sufficient benefit to continue it -- not that there was no criticism, nor that renewal happened against their own wishes.

quiz.q: A historian argues that a famine in a particular region was worsened by government policy, not solely by weather. Which finding would most directly support this claim?
o: The region experienced a severe drought that year.
Government records show grain exports from the region continued at normal levels throughout the famine.
The famine lasted for two years.
Neighboring regions also experienced poor harvests.
quiz.e: Continued grain EXPORTS during a famine directly points to a policy factor (not just weather) worsening the crisis -- the other choices only describe weather-related conditions.

quiz.q: The treaty was intended to bring lasting peace, but its vague language left key terms open to ______, which different parties later interpreted in conflicting ways. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: "Vague language" leading to being read "in conflicting ways" by different parties describes open "interpretation"; the other words don't match ambiguity being read differently by different people.

quiz.q: A community garden began charging a small annual fee after years of running entirely on donations, which had become unpredictable. Which choice best states the main idea?
o: The garden closed due to lack of funding.
The garden adopted a more predictable funding model after relying on inconsistent donations.
Donations to the garden increased sharply.
The garden no longer accepts donations.
quiz.e: The text describes a shift from unpredictable donations to a fee -- a move toward predictability, not closure or an outright ban on donations.

quiz.q: After weeks of ______ negotiations, the two companies finally reached an agreement just before the deadline. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
quiz.e: "Weeks of" negotiation before finally reaching agreement "just before the deadline" implies a long, difficult process -- "protracted" fits; the others suggest quickness or ease, which contradicts "weeks."

quiz.q: A small bookstore began hosting weekly author events after noticing that customers who attended a one-time event were more likely to return within the following month. Based on the text, which is the most reasonable inference?
o: The bookstore was losing money before the events began.
The bookstore likely expected the weekly events to increase repeat customer visits.
Author events are the bookstore's only source of revenue.
quiz.e: Given the pattern they noticed (event attendees returned more) and their resulting action (hosting more events), it's reasonable to infer they expected increased repeat visits -- not revenue-loss or dislike claims unsupported by the text.

quiz.q: A claim states that a company's four-day workweek trial improved employee productivity. Which finding would most directly support this claim?
o: Employees reported liking the extra day off.
Output per employee, measured by completed projects, rose 15% during the trial compared to the previous quarter.
quiz.e: A direct, measured increase in output (completed projects) is the clearest evidence for a productivity claim; employee sentiment, headcount, and duration don't measure productivity.

quiz.q: Birdwatchers in a coastal town counted fewer migrating warblers each spring from 2015 to 2022, while counts of resident sparrows stayed steady. Which choice best states the main idea?
o: All bird populations in the town declined.
Migrating warbler counts fell while resident sparrow counts did not.
quiz.e: The text reports two trends and makes no causal claim, so the answer simply restates them.

quiz.q: A historian notes that many early 20th-century factory workers kept diaries, but few diaries survive because families rarely preserved them. What does the text most strongly suggest?
o: Surviving diaries may not represent most workers' experiences.
quiz.e: If few survived, the survivors are a small, possibly unrepresentative sample.

quiz.q: A town replaced its streetlights with LED bulbs, cutting electricity use for lighting by 60%. The town's total electricity use fell only 2%. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Streetlights made up a small share of the town's electricity use.
The LED bulbs did not work.
Other buildings switched to LEDs too.
quiz.e: A large cut in one category barely changed the total, so that category must be small.

quiz.q: In her essay, a scientist argues that 'curiosity-driven research often produces the most useful discoveries, even when usefulness was never the goal.' Which example would best illustrate her claim?
o: A drug developed specifically to treat a known disease
A study of jellyfish glow that later led to a widely used medical imaging tool
A bridge designed to carry heavy traffic
A survey of voter opinions before an election
quiz.e: It shows research without a practical aim yielding a practical result.

quiz.q: A passage describes a novelist who revised each chapter 'until no sentence could be removed without loss.' The phrase mainly emphasizes the novelist's:
quiz.e: Removing everything unnecessary is a mark of concise, careful editing.

quiz.q: A study found that students who took notes by hand recalled more concepts than students who typed notes, but the typing group recorded more words. Which inference is best supported?
o: Typing is always harmful to learning.
Recording more words did not by itself lead to better recall.
quiz.e: More words didn't mean more recall; the study doesn't justify broader claims.

quiz.q: A researcher claims that urban trees lower summer street temperatures. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim?
o: Many residents say they enjoy trees.
Trees in cities live shorter lives than rural trees.
Streets with dense tree cover averaged 4°C cooler than similar streets without trees.
quiz.e: It directly compares temperature with and without trees while holding other factors similar.

quiz.q: A student claims that a poem's speaker feels isolated. Which quotation would best support this?
o: 'The morning sun is warm upon the stones.'
'We gathered at the table, laughing late.'
'The river bends toward the waiting sea.'
'I walk the crowded square, and no one knows my name.'
quiz.e: Being unknown in a crowd directly expresses isolation.

quiz.q: A table shows that a city's bike-share trips rose from 20,000 in 2019 to 55,000 in 2023, while bus trips fell slightly. Which claim does the data best support?
o: Everyone in the city now rides bikes.
Bike-share use grew substantially over the period.
Bike-share caused the drop in bus trips.
quiz.e: The data shows growth; it can't establish cause.

quiz.q: An economist claims that a sugar tax reduced soda purchases. Which finding would most weaken this claim?
o: Soda purchases fell by the same amount in nearby cities without the tax.
Soda prices rose after the tax.
The tax raised revenue for schools.
quiz.e: If purchases fell equally without the tax, something other than the tax likely caused the drop.

quiz.q: A graph shows average sleep for teens fell from 8.1 hours in 2010 to 7.4 hours in 2020. Which statement accurately describes the graph?
o: Teens slept less than 7 hours in 2020.
Average teen sleep decreased by 0.7 hours over the decade.
quiz.e: 8.1 − 7.4 = 0.7, and it's an average, not every teen.

quiz.q: A biologist claims a frog species breeds only after heavy rain. Which observation would most strengthen the claim?
o: Across 10 years, egg masses appeared only within days after storms exceeding 5 cm of rain.
The frogs are more active at night.
The frogs' habitat is a wetland.
Other frog species breed in spring.
quiz.e: It links breeding consistently to heavy rain over many years.

quiz.q: The engineer's explanation was so ______ that even visitors with no technical background understood it immediately. Which word best completes the text?
quiz.e: Lucid means clear and easy to understand.

quiz.q: Although the town's population was small, its annual festival drew ______ crowds, often ten times the number of residents. Which word best completes the text?
quiz.e: Ten times the population signals very large crowds.

quiz.q: The critic called the film ______, arguing that it copied the plot, characters and even dialogue of an earlier movie. Which word best completes the text?
quiz.e: Derivative means imitative of earlier work.

quiz.q: Early reports were ______; some claimed the bridge was closed, while others said it was open. Which word best completes the text?
quiz.e: Reports that disagree are contradictory.

quiz.q: As used in the text, 'The committee will table the proposal until next month,' 'table' most nearly means:
quiz.e: In U.S. usage, to table a proposal is to set it aside for later.

quiz.q: The athlete's ______ training schedule, with practice every morning and evening for years, explained her success. Which word best completes the text?
quiz.e: Twice-daily practice for years is rigorous.

quiz.q: The museum expected a small crowd for the exhibit. ______, over 5,000 visitors attended on opening day. Which transition best completes the text?
quiz.e: The outcome contrasts with the expectation.

quiz.q: Solar panels have become far cheaper over the past decade. ______, more homeowners are installing them. Which transition best completes the text?
quiz.e: Lower cost leads to more installations: cause and effect.

quiz.q: A student's notes: • The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system. • It stretches about 2,300 km. • It lies off Queensland, Australia. The student wants to emphasize the reef's size. Which choice does this best?
o: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Queensland, Australia.
Coral reefs exist in many oceans.
The Great Barrier Reef, stretching about 2,300 km, is the world's largest coral reef system.
quiz.e: It combines the facts that convey size.

quiz.q: Many desert plants store water in thick stems. ______, cacti can survive months without rain. Which transition best completes the text?
quiz.e: Cacti are an example of plants that store water.

quiz.q: The recipe calls for fresh basil. ______, dried basil can be used if fresh isn't available. Which transition best completes the text?
quiz.e: It introduces an alternative that contrasts with the instruction.

quiz.q: A student's notes: • Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911). • She was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences. The student wants to highlight Curie's unique achievement. Which choice does this best?
o: Marie Curie won a Nobel Prize in 1903.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded in 1911.
Marie Curie was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry.
quiz.e: It states the 'first ever' achievement directly.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'The list of required supplies ______ on the class website.'
quiz.e: The subject is 'list' (singular), not 'supplies'.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'The hikers packed three essentials ______ water, a map, and a first-aid kit.'
quiz.e: A colon introduces a list after a complete clause.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'The storm knocked out power across the city ______ most schools closed the next day.'
quiz.e: Two independent clauses can be joined by a semicolon; a comma alone creates a splice.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'Each of the students ______ a project to present.'
quiz.e: 'Each' is singular.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'The company announced ______ new policy yesterday.'
quiz.e: The possessive of 'it' is 'its'; 'it's' means 'it is'.

quiz.q: Which choice conforms to Standard English? 'Walking into the room, ______'
o: the new paintings caught Maria's eye.
Maria noticed the new paintings on the wall.
quiz.e: The modifier 'Walking into the room' must describe the subject, Maria, to avoid a dangling modifier.

quiz.q: A study found that honeybees exposed to a common pesticide took longer to find their way back to the hive. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The pesticide may impair honeybees' navigation.
Hives were destroyed by the pesticide.
quiz.e: Longer return times suggest navigation problems; the other claims go beyond the data.

quiz.q: Researchers noted that a deep-sea fish has eyes sensitive to red light, though little red light reaches that depth. They suspect the fish produces its own red light. Which finding would best support this?
o: The fish has organs that emit red light.
Red light travels far in shallow water.
quiz.e: Evidence of red light production directly supports the hypothesis.

quiz.q: A science passage uses 'In one trial…in a second trial…in both trials' to describe results. The main function of this structure is to:
o: Describe the history of the field
Show that a result was repeated
quiz.e: Repeated trials strengthen a finding.

quiz.q: A researcher claims that a plant grows taller in blue light than red light. Which experimental design would best test this?
o: Grow one plant in blue light only.
Grow identical plants under blue or red light with all other conditions equal, and compare heights.
quiz.e: A controlled comparison isolates light color.

quiz.q: A passage states a hypothesis 'remains untested because the necessary instruments do not yet exist.' This most strongly suggests the hypothesis:
o: Is based on a completed study
Has not been confirmed or disproven
quiz.e: Untested means neither confirmed nor refuted.

quiz.q: Data show a lake's average summer temperature rose 1.5°C over 30 years while its fish population fell 40%. Which statement is most justified?
o: Warming definitely caused the fish decline.
The two trends occurred over the same period, but the data alone don't show that warming caused the decline.
quiz.e: Correlation in time doesn't establish cause.

quiz.q: A historian claims that railroads helped standardize time in the United States. Which evidence best supports this?
o: Railroad companies adopted standard time zones in 1883 to coordinate schedules, before Congress made them official.
quiz.e: It directly connects railroads to adopting standard time.

quiz.q: A passage from an 1850s speech argues for women's property rights. The speaker's main purpose is most likely to:
o: Describe the history of property law neutrally
Persuade listeners to support legal change
quiz.e: Arguing for rights is persuasive.

quiz.q: An economist notes that a country's exports rose after its currency weakened. Which explanation is most consistent with basic economics?
o: A weaker currency made imports cheaper.
A weaker currency made the country's goods cheaper for foreign buyers.
quiz.e: Depreciation lowers the foreign price of exports.

quiz.q: Two historians disagree: one says a revolution was caused mainly by economic hardship; the other says mainly by new political ideas. Both would most likely agree that:
o: The revolution had identifiable causes worth explaining
quiz.e: They disagree on which cause mattered most, not on whether causes exist.

quiz.q: A social scientist found that neighborhoods with more parks reported higher community satisfaction, even after accounting for income. What does 'accounting for income' most likely accomplish?
o: It reduces the chance that income explains the relationship
It shows income doesn't matter to anyone
quiz.e: Controlling for a confounder strengthens, but doesn't prove, the link.

quiz.q: A historian writes that a letter 'must be read alongside the author's public speeches, which often contradicted it.' The historian's point is that:
o: Letters are always more honest than speeches
Sources should be interpreted in context with other evidence
quiz.e: Comparing sources gives a fuller picture.

quiz.q: You have 3 minutes left and two unanswered questions: one long evidence question and one short vocabulary question. The best strategy is to:
o: Spend all 3 minutes on the long one
Answer the quick vocabulary question first, then attempt the other
quiz.e: Secure the faster points first; there's no penalty for guessing.

quiz.q: On the digital SAT, is there a penalty for wrong answers?
quiz.e: Unanswered questions score the same as wrong ones, so never leave blanks.

quiz.q: For a 'best completes the text' vocabulary question, a good first step is to:
o: Predict your own word from context before reading the choices
quiz.e: Predicting avoids being swayed by distractors.

quiz.q: The digital SAT is adaptive, which means:
o: Every student sees the same questions
Questions get easier after a wrong answer
You can skip the second module
The second module's difficulty depends on performance in the first
quiz.e: Module 2 adapts based on Module 1.

quiz.q: For grammar questions, a useful strategy is to:
o: Pick the choice that sounds fanciest
Choose the answer with the most commas
Identify the rule being tested (agreement, punctuation, modifier) before choosing
quiz.e: Knowing the rule makes the correct choice clear.

quiz.q: When two answer choices both seem right on an evidence question, you should:
o: Pick the one with more numbers
Pick the one that most directly supports the specific claim
Pick the one with the most words
quiz.e: The best evidence is the most direct and relevant.

flashcards.d: The single controlling point a passage as a whole makes; must be supported by every part of the passage, not just one detail.
Why the author wrote the passage (to inform, argue, describe, compare) — tested by the verb in answer choices.
A specific fact or example explicitly stated in the passage that backs up the central idea.
A logical conclusion implied but not directly stated by the text; must be provable from the passage alone.
The author's own attitude or viewpoint toward the subject, shown through word choice and framing.
A restatement of a sentence's meaning in different words that preserves its original logical relationships.
A wrong-answer pattern using words like 'always,' 'never,' or 'proves' when the passage is actually tentative or qualified.
An answer choice that is too broad or too narrow relative to what the passage actually claims.
Hedging words like 'may,' 'suggests,' or 'some' that limit how strong a claim in the passage really is.
The topic is what a passage is about in general; the main idea is the specific point it makes about that topic.
Skill of identifying which quotation, detail, or data point best supports a specific claim or answer.
The textual support that most directly and specifically proves the claim in question, not just a related fact.
Data from a table, graph, or chart used to support or challenge a claim made in the passage.
To provide a fact that makes the claim more likely to be true, often by ruling out an alternative explanation.
To provide a fact that introduces doubt, an exception, or an alternative explanation for the claim.
Two variables changing together (correlation) does not by itself prove one causes the other (causation).
A true, on-topic fact that doesn't actually address or prove the specific claim being tested.
Whether a data trend is increasing, decreasing, or stable — must match the direction claimed in the text.
A data-reasoning trap where a claim about a large group is 'proven' using data from too small or narrow a sample.
An answer choice that supports the opposite of what the question actually asks for.
Question type asking for the meaning of a word/phrase as used in a specific sentence, or the best word to fill a blank.
Strategy of covering answer choices and predicting your own word for the blank before comparing to options.
The emotional or attitudinal association of a word (positive, negative, neutral) beyond its literal definition.
A word or phrase nearby in the sentence that reveals the meaning of the blank or targeted word.
Words like 'however,' 'yet,' 'although' that signal the blank should mean the opposite of a nearby idea.
Words like 'moreover,' 'similarly,' 'furthermore' that signal the blank should reinforce a nearby idea.
A word with more than one definition (e.g., 'sound,' 'novel') where context determines which meaning applies.
The level of formality (academic, casual, technical) a word choice must match to fit the passage.
A wrong choice that is a near-synonym but has the wrong degree of intensity for the sentence's context.
A word whose primary function is signaling the writer's or speaker's attitude, e.g., 'skeptical' or 'admiring.'
Using given bullet-point notes to construct the sentence that best fulfills a specific stated rhetorical goal.
A word or phrase showing the logical relationship (contrast, cause, addition) between two ideas or sentences.
Writing that expresses an idea in the fewest necessary words without losing meaning or grammatical correctness.
Unnecessary repetition of an idea already stated, e.g., 'return back' or 'each individual person.'
The specific function (e.g., 'to illustrate a contrast') a question asks a sentence to serve — the basis for add/delete questions.
A word like 'although,' 'because,' or 'while' that joins a dependent clause to an independent clause.
For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So — joins two independent, equally weighted clauses.
A descriptive phrase positioned so it appears to modify the wrong word in the sentence.
Words like 'therefore,' 'thus,' or 'consequently' signaling one idea results from another.
An answer that is factually accurate but doesn't accomplish the specific goal stated in the question.
The rule that a verb must match its true subject in number, ignoring intervening prepositional phrases.
An error joining two independent clauses with only a comma, e.g., 'It rained, we left.'
Two independent clauses joined with no punctuation or conjunction at all.
A group of words missing a subject or verb, or a subordinate clause standing alone, that cannot stand as a complete sentence.
A 'that' clause defining which specific noun is meant; takes no surrounding commas.
A 'which' clause adding extra, non-defining information; set off by commas.
The rule that items in a list, comparison, or joined by a conjunction must share the same grammatical form.
A pronoun must match its antecedent in number and gender, and refer unambiguously to one noun.
Subject pronouns (I, he, they, who) act as the subject; object pronouns (me, him, them, whom) act as the object.
A colon must follow a complete independent clause and introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration.
A researcher's testable prediction about an outcome, distinct from the actual findings of a study.
The factor a researcher deliberately manipulates in an experiment.
The outcome or measurement that changes in response to the independent variable.
A comparison group that does not receive the treatment, used to isolate the effect of the independent variable.
Research observing a relationship between variables without manipulating them, which cannot establish causation alone.
An unaccounted-for factor that offers an alternative explanation for an observed result.
A technical term meaning a result is unlikely to be due to random chance, distinct from everyday 'important.'
Findings are what a study observed; interpretation is the researcher's explanation of why it happened.
The explanation for HOW or WHY an observed scientific effect occurs, often signaled by 'because' or 'due to.'
A data point that doesn't fit the overall trend, often the focus of an 'except' or exception-based question.
A firsthand historical document or account written by someone present at or involved in the events described.
A modern or later analysis/commentary about a primary source or historical event.
An author's acknowledgment of a valid opposing point, often introduced with 'while it is true that...'
An opposing viewpoint an author raises, typically in order to refute or qualify it.
Word choice carrying strong positive or negative connotation that reveals bias, e.g., 'regime' vs. 'government.'
An author's overall position or attitude toward the subject, inferable from framing and word choice.
Two related passages presenting different perspectives on the same topic, compared for agreement/disagreement.
A question posed for persuasive effect, not to elicit an actual answer.
A point of agreement between two passages that otherwise reach different conclusions.
Dates, named events, or institutions in a passage that reveal the stakes of an argument without needing outside knowledge.
The Reading & Writing section's two 27-question, 32-minute modules; Module 2's difficulty adapts based on Module 1 performance.
A test format where performance on an earlier section/module determines the difficulty of a later one.
Roughly 60-75 seconds per question on average across a 27-question, 32-minute module.
Digital SAT tool marking a question to revisit later within the same module before submitting.
The digital SAT does not subtract points for wrong answers, so every question should get a guess.
Systematically ruling out unsupported, extreme, or off-topic choices rather than searching for a 'perfect' answer directly.
Deciding quickly which questions to answer immediately, flag, or guess-and-move-on based on difficulty and time.
Declining focus/accuracy over a long module of dense, unrelated passages; managed by mental resets between questions.
The digital SAT's end-of-module screen showing which questions are answered, unanswered, or flagged.
A self-imposed pacing check (e.g., at question 7, 14, 20) to confirm you're on schedule within a module.

PART_A.q: The critic's review was scathing, dismissing the film's dialogue as ______ and its plot as derivative. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
PART_A.e: "Scathing" and "dismissing" signal criticism, so the missing word should also be negative. "Stilted" (unnatural, awkward) fits; the others are neutral or positive.

PART_A.q: Marine biologist Sylvia Earle has spent over 7,000 hours underwater and led more than 100 ocean expeditions. Her research helped establish several marine protected areas, and she continues to advocate for ocean conservation into her late eighties. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To criticize past ocean conservation efforts
To describe the extensive career and continuing advocacy of a marine biologist
To compare Sylvia Earle's methods to those of other scientists
To argue that marine protected areas are ineffective
PART_A.e: The text simply describes Earle's career (hours underwater, expeditions, advocacy) — a straightforward summary, not a criticism, comparison, or argument.

PART_A.q: A researcher claims that a newly discovered moth species is nocturnal. Which finding, if true, would most directly support this claim?
